I farm a small 3 mu wheat-maize rotation in Quzhou, and with 40 years in the field I would keep the system steady rather than chase the highest possible input level. I have well irrigation, so I would protect wheat first because that season is drier here and water matters more then. For wheat, I would use an improved variety, put on a moderate fertilizer rate, rotary-till, and plan two irrigations: one around sowing if soil moisture is short, and one at jointing. I would not push nitrogen too high because in our North China Plain system too much N is common and often wasteful; I would rather aim for a stable stand, firm tillering, and fewer losses. I would expect a solid but not extreme wheat yield.

For summer maize, I would stay with hybrid seed because that is the straightforward way for me to keep yield stable on a small plot. After wheat harvest, I would keep soil disturbance low and go with no-tillage or very light disturbance so I can sow quickly and keep moisture. Summer rain usually carries much of the maize season here, so with a well available I would plan one irrigation mainly as insurance if establishment is dry or rain comes late. I would keep fertilizer below the heavy traditional level, especially nitrogen, because maize can use residual fertility from the wheat season and I do not want to spend more than the field can return. I would spray only as needed for weeds and then for insects or disease if pressure shows up. This is the balance I would choose: stable double-cropping, controlled water use, moderate fertilizer, and dependable output on 3 mu. I’m grounding that on North China Plain and Quzhou-area evidence that wheat usually needs the key irrigation focus, reduced-to-moderate N can hold yield better than conventional excess, and Quzhou’s wheat-maize system is already a high-output rotation. Sources: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378377424000611, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-019-55913-1, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5290742/
